pos: n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1183, beside the field of the battle of 1664 that checked the Ottoman advance)
etymology: Hungarian Szent Gotthard, Saint Gotthard, for Gotthard of Hildesheim.
biblical_def: Szentgotthard in western Hungary was founded in 1183 by Bela III and settled from Trois-Fontaines in Champagne. The abbey was wrecked in the Ottoman wars and rebuilt in the eighteenth century by the Cistercians of Heiligenkreuz, with a church painted by Stephan Dorffmaister whose ceiling shows the event that made the name famous: on the first of August 1664 an imperial and allied army under Montecuccoli beat a far larger Ottoman force on the Raab beside the abbey, the first real check to Ottoman arms in Hungary in a century and a half. The dictionary records Szentgotthard because a monastery that paints its own battle on its ceiling has to be asked where it thinks deliverance comes from. Zechariah answers the question before it is put, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). The posture required of those who are delivered is stillness and acknowledgement, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10). The terms on which a land is healed begin with humiliation rather than with a victory column, “shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face” (2Ch 7:14), and the peace that follows is the fruit of righteousness and not of artillery, “And the work of righteousness shall be peace” (Isa 32:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a battle as a fight between enemies; deliverance as release, rescue; might as strength, force; a victory as the defeat of an enemy; and peace as freedom from war.
webster_full: BATTLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression or any restraint; rescue from danger.
MIGHT, n. Strength; force; power; ability to perform.
VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from war with a foreign nation.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.
corruption_summary: Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1183 beside the field where the Ottoman advance was checked in 1664.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that deliverance is credited where Scripture credits it. Szentgotthard painted its own battle on its ceiling, and the prophet had already ruled out both of the explanations an army would offer, “Not by might, nor by power” (Zec 4:6).

The live temptation is a thanksgiving that functions as self-congratulation, which is what a victory church very easily becomes. The psalmist prescribes a posture rather than a monument, “I will be exalted among the heathen” (Psa 46:10); the healing of a land is conditioned on repentance, “and turn from their wicked ways” (2Ch 7:14); and the peace that lasts grows from righteousness, “quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17).

pos: n. (the Hungarian Cistercian abbey of 1232, whose church is the only intact medieval Cistercian church in Hungary)
etymology: Hungarian Bel-apat-falva, the village of the abbot of Bel, from apat, an abbot.
biblical_def: Belapatfalva under the Bukk hills was founded in 1232 by Bishop Kilit of Eger and settled from Pilis, and it is the one place in Hungary where a medieval Cistercian church still stands whole. Everything else of the order in the kingdom was destroyed in the Ottoman wars or rebuilt beyond recognition; this one, small and plain, with a Romanesque west front and the austere unornamented interior the early statutes required, came through and was carefully restored in the twentieth century. The conventual buildings are gone. The dictionary records Belapatfalva as the survivor, and as the standing rebuke to the habit of reading survival as approval. Christ said of a far greater building that not one stone would be left on another, “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2), so the loss of the rest proves nothing against them. The psalmist's lament over a ruined sanctuary is a lament and not a verdict, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” (Psa 74:7). What is promised to be immovable is not a church but a tent pitched by God, “a tabernacle that shall not be taken down” (Isa 33:20), and where men cease to speak of such things the material is said to be fit to testify, “if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out” (Luk 19:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to survive as to outlive; austere as rigid, severe; restoration as the act of replacing in a former state; a nave as the body of a church; and intact as untouched, entire.
webster_full: SURVIVE, v.t. To outlive; to live beyond the life of another; to live after any thing else.
AUSTERE, adj. Severe; harsh; rigid; stern; applied to persons, also to discipline and manner of life.
RESTORATION, n. The act of replacing in a former state; renewal; re-establishment.
NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the baluster or railing of the door to the chief choir.
ENTIRE, adj. Whole; undivided; unbroken; complete in its parts.
scriptures: Mat 24:2
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
Psa 74:7
They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground.

Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities: thine eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of the stakes thereof shall ever be removed, neither shall any of the cords thereof be broken.
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
corruption_summary: The only intact medieval Cistercian church in Hungary, founded 1232 from Pilis and restored in the twentieth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that survival is not approval. Belapatfalva stands and its sister houses do not, and Christ's own word about the temple forbids drawing conclusions about merit from masonry, “See ye not all these things?” (Mat 24:2).

The live temptation is a sentimental reading of ruin and remainder alike, in which the stones become the story. The psalmist treats a burnt sanctuary as grief rather than as judgment on its builders, “the dwelling place of thy name to the ground” (Psa 74:7); the one structure promised permanence is pitched by God and not by an order, “Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities” (Isa 33:20); and the testimony that matters can be given by stones only when men fall silent, “I tell you that” (Luk 19:40).

pos: n. (the Transylvanian Cistercian abbey of about 1202, dissolved in 1474 and since Lutheran)
etymology: Hungarian Kerc, Romanian Carta, German Kerz, from a local place-name.
biblical_def: Kerc on the Olt in Transylvania was founded about 1202 and settled from Igris, the southernmost Cistercian house in the kingdom of Hungary, planted among the Transylvanian Saxons. It was repeatedly raided, and in 1474 Matthias Corvinus dissolved it outright and gave its estates to the provost of Sibiu, the community having dwindled to almost nothing. The Saxon villagers kept the choir of the abbey church as their parish church; they accepted the Reformation in the sixteenth century, and it is a Lutheran parish church still, with the nave standing roofless beside it. The dictionary records Kerc because the transfer was from an order to a congregation, which is the right direction. A flock is committed to overseers and the price of it is named, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and the manner required of those overseers excludes both compulsion and profit, “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). The pastors God promises are competent to teach, “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15), and the one qualification that cannot be waived is possession of a message received, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parish as the precinct of a church; an overseer as one who superintends; a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church; lucre as gain in money; and a flock as a company of beasts, also a Christian congregation.
webster_full: PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the precinct the inhabitants of which belong to the same church.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a bishop; one who has the charge of a church.
PASTOR, n. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
LUCRE, n. Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: Transylvania's Cistercian abbey of about 1202, dissolved 1474, its choir kept as a Saxon parish church and Lutheran since the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church belongs to a congregation under pastors rather than to an order under an abbot. Kerc's choir passed to the Saxon villagers and is theirs still, and the apostolic charge over such a people names what they cost, “which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

The live temptation is an oversight exercised for the overseer's benefit, which is how the abbey emptied in the first place. Peter forbids both the coercion and the profit motive, “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (1Pe 5:2); the pastors God promises are men who can actually teach, “And I will give you pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15); and the irreducible qualification is a received message held fast, “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

pos: n. (the Danish Cistercian abbey of 1151, mother house of the order in the Baltic north)
etymology: Danish Esrum, from Esrum lake, perhaps the ash-tree room or clearing.
biblical_def: Esrum in north Zealand was made a Cistercian house in 1151 by Archbishop Eskil of Lund, settled from Clairvaux, and became the most important abbey in Denmark and the mother of houses across the Baltic: Sorø, Vitskøl, Kolbatz in Pomerania, Dargun in Mecklenburg. Its cartulary, the Esrum Book, survives. Eskil himself resigned the primacy of Denmark in 1177, went to Clairvaux and died there a monk. The abbey was dissolved in 1559 and one wing remains. The dictionary records Esrum for Eskil's resignation, which is the most interesting thing about it: an archbishop laying down the greatest office in his country. Christ commends a woman for choosing one thing over many, “But one thing is needful” (Luk 10:42), and the beatitude is spoken over a condition no primacy confers, “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3). Paul writes off advantages of a far better kind than an archbishopric, “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Phi 3:8). Yet the dictionary notes the limit: Eskil went to a cloister, and the patriarchs are commended for holding their whole earthly standing loosely wherever they stood, “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to resign as to give up a claim or office; a primate as the chief ecclesiastic; renunciation as the act of disowning; a cartulary as a register of a monastery; and to abdicate as to relinquish an office.
webster_full: RESIGN, v.t. To give up; to yield; to surrender; to relinquish a claim, office or commission.
PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
RENUNCIATION, n. The act of renouncing; a disowning; rejection.
CARTULARY, n. A register book, as of a monastery; a place where papers or records are kept.
ABDICATE, v.t. To relinquish an office before the expiration of the term; to give up a right.
scriptures: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Phi 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Denmark's chief Cistercian house, 1151, mother of Soro, Vitskol, Kolbatz and Dargun, whose founder resigned the primacy to die a monk.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an office is worth less than the one thing needful. Eskil of Lund gave up the primacy of Denmark and went to Clairvaux to die, and the Lord's commendation of such a choice is given to a woman sitting still, “which shall not be taken away from her” (Luk 10:42).

The live temptation is to read the cloister as the only place such a choice can be made, which is the error the Reformers corrected rather than the renunciation itself. The beatitude attaches to a disposition and not to an address, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3); Paul's reckoning is made in the middle of an active ministry, “for whom I have suffered the loss of all things” (Phi 3:8); and the patriarchs held everything loosely without leaving their tents, “These all died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:13).

pos: n. (the Jutland Cistercian abbey of 1158, whose monks drained the Bjornsholm marsh)
etymology: Danish Vitskol, perhaps from Vitae Schola, the school of life, the abbey's Latin style.
biblical_def: Vitskøl on the Limfjord in Jutland was founded in 1158 by Valdemar I and settled from Varnhem in Sweden, and its Latin name was Vitae Schola, the school of life. The monks drained the Bjørnsholm marsh with dykes and ditches, built a mill and a herring fishery, and held the largest monastic estate in north Jutland. It was dissolved in 1536 at the Danish Reformation, turned into a manor, and the medieval chapter house and part of the church survive. The dictionary records Vitskøl for its name and its ditches together, since the school of life taught drainage. Scripture does not separate the two: the apostolic rule in a community is that the unwilling worker goes hungry, “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and the proverb promises the spade a return that it denies to conversation, “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23). Small faithfulness is the assay of large trust, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luk 16:10), and the commendation at the end of such an estate names fidelity rather than acreage, “thou hast been faithful over a few things” (Mat 25:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dyke as a bank or mound to resist water; to drain as to draw off water gradually; a fen as low flat land covered with water; a fishery as the business of catching fish; and a mill as a machine for grinding.
webster_full: DIKE, n. A ditch; a channel for water made by digging; also, a mound of earth, of stones, raised to prevent low lands from being inundated.
DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to percolate; to draw off gradually, as water from land.
FEN, n. Low land covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses or other aquatic plants.
FISHERY, n. The business of catching fish; also, a place for catching fish.
MILL, n. A complicated engine or machine for grinding and reducing to fine particles, grain, fruit or other substance.
scriptures: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Jutland Cistercian abbey of 1158, styled Vitae Schola, whose monks drained the Bjornsholm marsh and held north Jutland's largest estate.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a school of life may properly teach drainage. Vitskøl dug dykes and called itself Vitae Schola without any sense of contradiction, and the apostolic rule in a Christian community is as practical as a ditch, “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you” (2Th 3:10).

The live temptation for a house with the largest estate in a province is competence without fidelity. The proverb promises the spade a return and idle talk nothing, “but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23); the Lord makes small accounts the assay of great ones, “and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much” (Luk 16:10); and the verdict at the reckoning names a quality rather than a quantity, “Well done, thou good and faithful servant” (Mat 25:21).

pos: n. (the South Jutland Cistercian abbey of 1173, whose brick church is now a Lutheran parish church and a school of church music)
etymology: Danish Logumkloster, the cloister at Logum, from kloster, a monastery.
biblical_def: Løgumkloster in South Jutland was founded in 1173 and settled from Herrevad, and its brick church, finished about 1325, is among the purest Cistercian buildings in Scandinavia: a plain cross-vaulted interior with almost no ornament, exactly as the early statutes of the order required. It was dissolved in 1548, and the church has served as a Lutheran parish church ever since. Since the twentieth century the town has held the Danish national school of church music and a retreat house, so that the building is once again full of singing it was built for. The dictionary records Løgumkloster for that continuity of praise through a change of doctrine. The noise proper to a relaid foundation is thanksgiving, “And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD” (Ezr 3:11), and the content of what is sung is a report handed to the next generation, “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). Persistence in prayer has thanksgiving as its appointed companion, “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2), and the posture of those who keep the hours is a watchman's, “more than they that watch for the morning” (Psa 130:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalm as a sacred song; a chant as a song, also to sing after the manner of a cathedral service; a hymn as a song of adoration to God; thanksgiving as the act of rendering thanks; and a choir as a band of singers.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
CHANT, v.t. To sing; to utter with a melodious voice; to sing after the manner of a cathedral service.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
CHOIR, n. A band or collection of singers; also, the part of a church appropriated to the singers.
scriptures: Ezr 3:11

And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Col 4:2
Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;
My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
corruption_summary: South Jutland Cistercian abbey of 1173, a Lutheran parish church since 1548 and now the Danish school of church music.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that praise survives a reformation of doctrine and ought to. Løgumkloster's plain vaults have been sung under for seven centuries, Cistercian and then Lutheran, and the proper sound at a relaid foundation is exactly that, “because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid” (Ezr 3:11).

The live temptation is music that becomes its own object, which the Cistercians guarded against by building without ornament and modern choirs forget. The content of singing is a report, “and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done” (Psa 78:4); its companion in prayer is named, “and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2); and the posture of those who keep the hours is watchfulness rather than performance, “My soul waiteth for the Lord” (Psa 130:6).

pos: n. (the Scanian Cistercian abbey of 1144, the first house of the order in Scandinavia, and the site of Tycho Brahe's observation of the new star of 1572)
etymology: Old Danish Herrevad, the lord's ford, from herre and vad, a ford.
biblical_def: Herrevad in Scania was founded in 1144 by Archbishop Eskil and settled directly from Clairvaux, the first Cistercian house anywhere in Scandinavia and the parent of Løgumkloster and others. It was dissolved at the Danish Reformation and granted out; and on the evening of the eleventh of November 1572, standing in its grounds, the young Tycho Brahe saw a star in Cassiopeia that had not been there, the supernova whose measurement overturned the doctrine that the heavens above the moon are changeless. He published it as De nova stella. The dictionary records Herrevad for that night, and for the order of knowing it illustrates. Brahe trusted an observation over an inherited system, which is the right instinct, and Scripture gives it a starting point, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10). The understanding so begun is tested by obedience, “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psa 111:10). The law of the LORD is held to be of a different order from a cosmology, “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7), and the light a man may actually steer by in the dark is a word rather than a star, “a light that shineth in a dark place” (2Pe 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a star as a luminous body in the heavens; a nova would be a new star; astronomy as the science of the heavenly bodies; a sphere as an orb, a globe; and observation as the act of noticing, the information so obtained.
webster_full: STAR, n. An apparently luminous or lucid body in the heavens; a heavenly body.
ASTRONOMY, n. The science which teaches the knowledge of the celestial bodies, their magnitudes, motions, distances and order.
SPHERE, n. An orbicular body; a globe; in astronomy, the concave expanse of the heavens.
OBSERVATION, n. The act of observing; notice; the information or notion gained by observing.
FIRMAMENT, n. The region of the air; the sky or heavens.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.

Psa 19:7

We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Scandinavia's first Cistercian house, 1144, where Tycho Brahe saw the new star of 1572 that overturned an unchanging heavens.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an observation may rightly overturn an inherited system, and that the ordering of knowledge still begins elsewhere. Brahe trusted his eyes against Aristotle in Herrevad's grounds, and the proverb names the starting point of all such work, “and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Pro 9:10).

The live temptation is to let the instrument become the authority, so that measurement decides what may be believed. Scripture tests understanding by obedience rather than by acuteness, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Psa 111:10); it claims for the law of the LORD an effect no cosmology has, “the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7); and the dependable light in the dark is a word and not a new star, “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed” (2Pe 1:19).

pos: n. (the Swedish Cistercian abbey of 1143, the first in Sweden, where Birgitta of Sweden lived and claimed revelations)
etymology: Old Swedish Alvastra, from alver, elves, or a local root; latinised Alvastrum.
biblical_def: Alvastra in Östergötland was founded in 1143 and settled directly from Clairvaux, on the same day as Nydala, the two being the first Cistercian houses in Sweden. Its best-known connection is Birgitta Birgersdotter, later Birgitta of Sweden: her husband Ulf died at Alvastra in 1344, she stayed on in a house by the abbey for some years, and it was there that she began to dictate the visions published as the Revelationes, which she said were given her by Christ and the Virgin, and which carried political instructions to popes and kings. She founded the Bridgettine order and was canonised in 1391. The dictionary honours her courage in addressing the powerful and names the claim itself as the corruption. A revelation that arrives after the apostles is tested, not received, and the test is a written one, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20), applied against a deposit already closed, “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The standard is set so high that no messenger whatever is exempt from it, “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8), and Peter, who had seen Christ transfigured with his own eyes, still ranked the written word above that experience, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19). Her courage may be honoured. Her visions may not be believed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revelation as the act of disclosing what was before unknown, especially divine truth; a vision as something apparently seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; a visionary as one who is given to reveries; canonization as the act of declaring a saint; and the canon as the genuine books of Scripture.
webster_full: REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them; especially, the direct communication of truth to men by God.
VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; also, something imaginary; a phantom; a supernatural appearance.
VISIONARY, n. One who is given to reverie; one who forms impracticable schemes; one whose imagination is disturbed.
CANONIZATION, n. The act of declaring a man a saint, or of ranking a deceased person in the catalogue of saints.
CANON, n. In theology, the genuine books of the Holy Scriptures, called the sacred canon or rule of faith.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: Sweden's first Cistercian house, 1143, where Birgitta of Sweden began dictating the revelations that founded the Bridgettine order.
corruption_paragraphs: Birgitta of Sweden told popes to return to Rome and kings to stop their wars, and the dictionary grants her the courage that took. What she claimed for her authority is the problem. The Revelationes are presented as the words of Christ and of the Virgin given directly to her, and that claim puts them where only one kind of writing stands. Scripture provides a test rather than a welcome, “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).

Rome canonised her in 1391 and still reckons such private revelations as worthy of belief though not binding, which concedes the principle while softening the edge. Scripture closes the deposit, “it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you” (Jud 1:3), and sets the standard so high that no messenger is exempt from it, “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you” (Gal 1:8). Peter, who had seen Christ transfigured, ranked the written word above that experience, “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19).

pos: n. (the Swedish Cistercian abbey of 1143 in Smaland, whose abbot and monks were drowned in 1521)
etymology: Swedish Nydala, the new valley, from ny and dal; latinised Nova Vallis.
biblical_def: Nydala in Småland was founded in 1143 from Clairvaux on the same day as Alvastra, and its name is the Cistercian habit of hopeful naming: the new valley. The monks drained the lakeside, built a brick and stone church, and held a modest estate. In 1521, during the war that brought Gustav Vasa to the Swedish throne, the Danish commander Didrik Slagheck had the abbot and a number of the monks taken out onto the ice of Lake Rusken and drowned. The house never recovered and was dissolved in 1529; the church survives as a parish church. The dictionary records Nydala for that killing, because it is the point at which a story about granges and ditches becomes a story about suffering. The figure Scripture gives for a life under such conditions is a long race run among witnesses, “let us run with patience the race that is set before us” (Heb 12:1), and the blessing is pronounced on a condition rather than an outcome, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Mat 5:3). Religion that God accepts is measured by whom it attends to in affliction, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), and the instruction for the years after a disaster is to wait, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines martyrdom as the death of a martyr; affliction as the state of being afflicted, calamity; patience as the suffering of afflictions with calmness; to drown as to deprive of life by immersion; and a valley as a hollow between hills.
webster_full: MARTYRDOM, n. The death of a martyr; the suffering of death on account of adherence to the Christian faith.
AFFLICTION, n. The cause of continued pain of body or mind; calamity; a state of pain, distress or grief.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance.
DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to deprive of life by immersion in water or other fluid.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Lam 3:26
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Swedish Cistercian house of 1143 whose abbot and monks were drowned under the ice of Lake Rusken in 1521.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the history of a religious house is finally a history of people. Nydala's abbot was drowned under the ice in 1521, and the figure Scripture gives a life lived out under such conditions is a race run with endurance, “so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1).

The live temptation is to turn a killing into a cult, which is how a martyrology displaces a Bible. Scripture keeps the blessing on a disposition rather than on a death, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3); it measures acceptable religion by whom it visits, “and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27); and the instruction for the long aftermath is neither vengeance nor commemoration but waiting, “and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

pos: n. (the Swedish Cistercian abbey of 1150 in Vastergotland, burial church of Birger Jarl, restored in the seventeenth century)
etymology: Old Swedish Varnhem, the sheltered home, from a root for protection and hem, a home.
biblical_def: Varnhem in Västergötland was founded in 1150 from Alvastra on land given by a noblewoman named Sigrid, and became the burial church of Birger Jarl, the founder of Stockholm, and of King Erik Eriksson. Excavation under the church has found Christian graves from about the year 1000, two centuries before the abbey, which makes Varnhem one of the earliest Christian sites in Sweden. It was dissolved at the Reformation, burned, and lay roofless until Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie rebuilt and re-roofed it in the 1660s as his own burial church. It is a parish church still. The dictionary records Varnhem for that rescue, because the rebuilding of a roofless church is a scriptural office with a promise attached, “And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations” (Isa 61:4). The glory of a second house is promised in terms that exceed the first, “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former” (Hag 2:9), and the agency is God's before it is a count's, “When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory” (Psa 102:16). The tombs under its floor leave the one question a burial church exists to raise, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a jarl would be an earl, a nobleman; a sepulchre as a grave or tomb; to re-edify as to rebuild; a patron as one who supports or protects; and excavation as the act of hollowing out.
webster_full: EARL, n. A British title of nobility, or a nobleman, the third in rank, being next below a marquis.
SEPULCHRE, n. A grave; a tomb; the place where a dead body is interred, or deposited.
RE-EDIFY, v.t. To rebuild; to build anew after destruction.
PATRON, n. A protector; one who countenances or supports; an advocate; a defender.
EXCAVATION, n. The act of excavating, or making hollow; a hollow or a cavity formed by removing the interior substance.
scriptures: Isa 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
Hag 2:9
The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts: and in this place will I give peace, saith the LORD of hosts.
When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.
If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
corruption_summary: Swedish Cistercian abbey of 1150, burial church of Birger Jarl, roofless after the Reformation and rebuilt in the 1660s.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that re-roofing a ruined church is honourable work with a word spoken over it. Varnhem lay open to the weather for a century and De la Gardie rebuilt it, and the promise attached to such labour is explicit, “they shall repair the waste cities” (Isa 61:4).

The live temptation is the patron's, which is to rebuild a church chiefly as a place to be buried in. Haggai's promise about a second house is spoken by God and not by the donor, “saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:9); the psalmist assigns the agency plainly, “When the LORD shall build up Zion” (Psa 102:16); and the graves in the floor put the question no endowment answers, “all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come” (Job 14:14).
